hero.name: Abhishek
hero.who: a Class 12 student in Patna whose attention seems to vanish every evening

story.b: Abhishek sits down at seven with his physics book and a cup of tea. By seven twelve, he has checked the class group, watched one cricket clip and replied to a cousin. At nine, he has read four pages and remembers none of them. His board exams are in March. Downstairs the television plays a loud serial, a neighbour's generator hums, and his phone lights up every few minutes. His mother says he lacks concentration. His tuition sir says this generation is lazy. Abhishek starts to agree. In Class 7 he used to finish thick adventure novels in one sitting. Now he cannot hold one paragraph, and he decides the problem is simply him.

ask.q: Abhishek has decided he simply cannot concentrate. What is the most useful thing for him to do first?
o: Accept it and lower his targets for the board exams
Watch one evening closely and note what actually interrupts him
Watch motivational videos until he feels fired up again
ask.why: Before blaming himself, he needs to see what is really happening at his desk. Noting each interruption turns a vague feeling into problems he can fix. Lowering his targets accepts defeat too early, and motivational videos are one more distraction that fades by the next evening.

chapters.take: Before you call yourself lazy, look at what is breaking your focus.

story.b: Abhishek takes a page and makes a mark for every interruption in one evening. By nine there are thirty-one marks. Most are not his fault alone. The phone pings with notifications he never asked for, from games, shopping apps and the class group. The television downstairs is loud enough to follow the serial's plot. His desk faces the window, where the neighbour's generator roars during power cuts. He sees that he has been trying to concentrate in a room full of things pulling him away. So he turns off every notification except calls, moves his desk to face the wall, and buys foam earplugs for twenty rupees from the chemist.

ask.q: His cousin Neha also says she has zero focus and blames herself. What should Abhishek suggest first?
o: List three things around her that steal her focus, and change one
Wake at four every day to prove she has discipline
Accept that she is just a distracted person
ask.why: Her surroundings are likely working against her, just as his were. Spotting and changing even one thief, like notifications or a noisy seat, gives her effort a fair chance. Waking at four tests willpower without removing the pulls, and calling herself distracted turns a fixable problem into an identity.

chapters.take: Your focus depends on your surroundings as well as your effort.

story.b: Abhishek notices how he studies. A chemistry problem, then a message, then back to the problem, where he has to read the question again. Then a reel a friend shared, then the problem, read a third time. It feels like two hours of hard work, but the page shows almost nothing. One Saturday he tries an experiment. He switches the phone off and leaves it with his mother in the kitchen. He keeps only the chemistry book and a notebook on the desk. For thirty minutes he does nothing else. He finishes eight problems, more than he managed in the whole previous evening, and he is less tired at the end.

ask.q: His friend Kunal says he can revise and chat at the same time without any loss. What is the honest reply?
o: It works as long as he replies fast and keeps the chats short
Multitasking is a skill, so he should simply practise it more
Every switch costs a small restart, so he will be slower and make more errors
ask.why: Jumping between tasks feels productive, but the brain has to reload each time. Short replies still force a restart, and practice does not remove that cost. Kunal will finish faster and with fewer mistakes by doing one thing at a time.

chapters.take: Switching feels busy, but every jump costs time and focus.

story.b: One evening Abhishek picks the integration problems from last year's question paper, the ones just beyond what he can comfortably do. He sets one goal: finish five before dinner. The first takes forty minutes and two wrong turns. The second clicks halfway through. Somewhere in the third, he stops noticing the generator noise. When his mother calls him for dinner, he looks up, confused that it is already nine. He has done four, and he wants to do the fifth. The next day he tries the same thing with easy revision questions he already knows well, and his mind drifts to the phone within ten minutes.

ask.q: Abhishek wants more evenings like the integration one. Which task should he set himself tomorrow?
o: Easy questions he already knows, so he feels confident and calm
One clear set of problems that matters to him and stretches him a little
The hardest paper in the book, to really test his limits
ask.why: Deep focus tends to come from a clear goal that matters and stretches you slightly. Easy questions bore the mind into wandering, and a paper far beyond him brings frustration rather than absorption. The sweet spot sits just past what feels comfortable.

chapters.take: Clear goals that stretch you a little open the door to deep focus.

story.h: Studying at one in the morning
story.b: To catch up, Abhishek has been studying until one at night and waking at six for tuition. In the afternoons, his eyes keep closing over the same paragraph. Everything distracts him: the fan, a horn outside, a fly on the wall. One week, mostly from exhaustion, he gives in and sleeps at eleven, with his phone charging in the living room. He also starts walking the fifteen minutes to tuition without earphones, just looking at the shops and rickshaws on Boring Road. He worries he is wasting time. But by Friday the afternoon fog has lifted, and during one quiet walk, the answer to a stuck physics problem arrives on its own.

ask.q: Kunal stays up till two revising and keeps losing focus in class. What should Abhishek suggest?
o: Sleep earlier with the phone outside the room, and see whether his focus improves
Drink extra tea in the afternoons to push through the tiredness
Study even later at night, since more hours means more revision
ask.why: A tired brain struggles to filter out distractions, so extra hours at night often buy less real learning. Sleeping earlier gives focus a chance to return. Tea may mask tiredness for a while without fixing it, and studying later deepens the very problem stealing his attention.

chapters.take: A rested mind usually focuses better than a tired one working longer.

story.b: Abhishek's own changes help, but the class group chat still buzzes with a hundred messages every evening. Leaving it is not an option, because teachers post notices there. He realises the problem is bigger than his own willpower. Everyone in the group is losing their evenings the same way. So he talks to the class monitor and two friends. Together they suggest a simple rule: no messages between seven and nine, except urgent notices from teachers. At home he asks his family whether the television could stay low during those hours, and offers to fetch the milk every morning in return. His father grumbles, then agrees.

ask.q: Abhishek's friends say the group chat noise is just how things are. What is the best response?
o: Quietly mute it and stop worrying about anyone else
Complain about it in the group and do nothing more
Propose a shared quiet time that everyone agrees to follow
ask.why: When a problem affects everyone, a shared agreement works better than each person fighting alone. A quiet window protects the whole class. Muting may help him a little, but his friends still lose their evenings, and complaining without proposing a change just adds more messages.

chapters.take: Some focus problems are shared, so the fixes need to be shared too.

story.b: In the last week of February, Abhishek's evenings look different. The phone rests in the living room from seven to nine and every night from eleven. The class group stays mostly quiet in those hours, and three classmates have told him their pre-board marks went up. His desk still faces the wall, the earplugs sit in a small tin, and the integration problems no longer scare him. He still gets distracted, some evenings badly. But he no longer calls himself lazy. When it happens, he looks around the room first and asks what pulled him away. His mother, who once said he lacked concentration, now lowers the television herself at seven.

chapters.take: Guard your attention with better surroundings, good sleep and shared rules, not willpower alone.
